For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors.  In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million. 

In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.

My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.  

I chose federal court.

Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places.  Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there.  For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.

posts.text:
THE LACK OF CAPITULATIONS AND WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT!?

On recent calls w SMB & KTG, I observed that stocks haven’t really been capitulating and that this makes for one of the trickiest market environments.

A slow market, you sit on your hands. But an active market that doesn’t quite setup is the most dangerous. Recently we’ve been seeing some massive moves, but nothing so juicy and nothing so capitulatory. But seductive, it is.

Probably since the “Leopold bottom” stocks have been getting overextended, closing weak, Making it so that you don't position long on the front side only to gap up the next day.

This happened a few weeks ago and with most of the semis, after yesterday's weak price action, it is happening again with today's gap up. Each time, you feel FOMO and question whether this will be the turn and you will have missed it. I think I am not alone when I say that there are many frustrated traders out there right now.

Most importantly, what does one do about it? I think there are a few options.

1. You can conclude that, due to the increase in overnight trading and global trading, there has been a structural change where sectors and stocks are not going to capitulate intraday as much anymore. This is a theory I am certainly keeping an eye on, but I am not so convinced just yet. If this does end up true, it makes trading the overnight sessions far more appealing and tempting, and it requires us to adapt our trading. 

2. The second option is: if this isn't a structural change, you can resist FOMO and sit on your hands, maintaining your high standard of selectivity and only getting involved when something truly sets up. This is largely where I currently sit and am not embarrassed to say it.  

3. Option three is somewhere in between. When stocks are overextended and closing weak, you can start to structure a front-side position, particularly appealing to do so using call options. My current view on this is really dependent on the implied volatility and the day of the week. On a Monday, I don't find this so particularly appealing. If there are weekly or monthly options, however, as you get closer and closer to a Friday, I do think this method is starting to have some appeal.

A lot of trading is observing and adapting to market structure changes. I do think that markets and position unwinds have increasingly come outside of market hours, but I'm also not negating the fact that we really haven't got that rip-your-face-off melt. If you're patient and not caught offside, that will more than make up for any of the FOMO now.

In a sense, right now I am at a data collection point. I'm observing, I'm thinking, and I'm talking to other traders. I'm not particularly ready to lower my standards or reach a new conclusion.

As I jokingly told a friend, after four or five times of missing these overnight bounces after a weak close, I'm going to position on the front side. That will be the time that we gap down and melt. It's a joke, but I think there's a lot of truth to that, which is why, ultimately, for now, I'm maintaining my process and selectivity. 

I would love to hear all of your thoughts on this.

France's Debt Problem Is Real. A Eurozone Crisis Is Not Inevitable.

Robin Brooks is right to sound the alarm over France's deteriorating fiscal position. But higher sovereign yields are not synonymous with an impending debt crisis.

France's 10-year borrowing costs now exceed Italy's, yet French debt retains market access, a long maturity profile and substantial investor demand. This looks more like a sharp repricing of country-specific fiscal and political risk than evidence of indiscriminate eurozone contagion.

An oil-price shock could certainly aggravate the situation. But the decisive variable is not oil alone. It is the interaction between growth, debt dynamics, fiscal credibility and the ECB's capacity to contain unjustified fragmentation.

The real danger is when fiscal paralysis turns a manageable debt problem into a self-reinforcing market crisis. That is the distinction policymakers must understand before it is too late.

Yes, but the basic problem is the Euro. It is a mechanism that overrode the normal equalizing mechanism that adjusts for structural differences between nations: The Exchange Rate.

For Instance: Previously, before the common currency destroyed the adjustment mechanism, each nation had its own currency that would rise or fall against each other based upon fundamental factors and structural differences. The average Greek retires on a publicly-funded pension at age 54 while a German worker retires at age 67. Some 46% of Greek workers are in the public sector and are funded by 54% who work in the private sector. In Germany, the ratio is closer to 35-65. The Greek budget is continuously in deep deficit while Germans are usually far less profligate.

These huge economic imbalances would normally have been equalized by a declining Drachma and a rising Mark. Now that adjusting function has been overridden.

This causes funds to flow into the Northern Tier economies out of the periphery because Euro-demoninated German assets are on sale while Euro-denominated Greek assets are wildly overpriced.

If the German Central Bank must be relied upon to fund periphery deficits, it's because the rules of the game were rigged in 1992 when this disastrous, unsustainable, absurd common currency mechanism was launched.

Don't cry for Germany. Undo the common currency and restore economic sanity. Then global investors can decide which countries are worth the risk, and which country-specific rate of return levels are justified.

1/This lawsuit could be significant and yes (hope you’re sitting down) it is by 6 large ERISA plan employers against @UHC.

While important & significant, there are allegations that UHC acting as a “third party administrator” of the employees’ claims used AI/bots to deny claims illegally and compensated its own physician owned practices better than the independent practices.

The most important allegations come from the plaintiffs allegations on “shared savings.”

Shared savings occur when an out of network (OON) claim is administered by a 3d party, e.g. formerly Multiplan, now called Claritev, it negotiates or recommends a lower fee for the OON services and Claritev then shares the “savings” (the delta between the charges and initial payment) w/ UHC.

One might ask—“why should this occur under the NSA as the QPA (initial payment) is set at the 2019 median allowed amount for that CPT adjusted by a +28% CPI-U?” 

That is what the NSA requires but we know from 3 CMS audits (2 released in the last 2 weeks) that the health plans are manipulating the QPAs downward (perhaps for shared savings), are not in compliance w/ QPA fee setting regs and not complying with QPA disclosure regs.

So, this case may importantly prove the axiom of the late great Charlie Munger:  “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the result.”
